summary:
Use two pointers on the same array: `read` visits every cell, `write` marks the end of the kept part. Each
non-blank cell is copied to `write`, which then advances. The first `write` cells are the answer, in order.
O(n) time, O(1) extra space.

question.md:
Remove every cell equal to `blank`, keep the others in order, and return them, ideally in place.

- **Order matters**: the kept cells stay in their original order.
- **Up to 10⁵ cells.**

**Edge cases to keep in mind**

- No blanks: the list is unchanged.
- All blanks: the result is empty.
- The kept cells must stay in their original order.

think.md:
**Why deleting by shifting is slow.** Removing one element from the middle of an array means moving everything after
it one step left: O(n) per deletion. With many deletions that's O(n²), even though each kept element only needs to
move once, straight to its final slot.

**The read/write idea.** One pointer, `read`, visits every element once. A second pointer, `write`, marks the end of
the part we're keeping, which always sits at the **front** of the array. Each kept element is copied to `a[write]`
and `write` moves on; a dropped element is simply not copied.

**Why it's safe to overwrite in place.** `write` never gets ahead of `read` (it moves at most once per element read),
so every write lands on a slot that has already been read. Nothing unread is ever lost.

**Invariant.** After reading the first `r` elements, `a[0 .. write)` holds exactly the elements that should be kept
among those `r`, in their original order.

approaches.title: Delete by shifting

idea.md: Scan the list; whenever a blank is found, shift everything after it one place left and shrink the length. Don't advance the index after a deletion, because a new element has moved into it.

build: On a blank, shift the tail left and shrink.

lines.text: A working copy, its current length and the scan position.
Look at each cell of the shrinking list.
A blank: slide the rest of the list left over it and shrink the length. The index stays, because the next cell now sits here.

complexity.md: **Time O(n²)** when many cells are blank. **Space O(1)** besides the copy.

steps.text: Blank at 1: shift the 5 cells after it left.
Blank at 2: shift the 3 cells after it left.
Blank at 2: shift the 2 cells after it left.

walk.title: Find a blank, delete it by shifting everything after it one place left, and repeat.

limits.md: Each deletion moves the whole tail. The read/write pass moves each kept cell once, straight to its final slot.

approaches.title: Read and write pointers

idea.md: Read every cell; copy each non-blank cell to `a[write]` and advance `write`. The answer is `a[0 .. write)`.

build: For each cell: if it isn't blank, `a[write] = cell`, `write += 1`.

lines.text: The write position starts at 0: nothing kept yet.
Visit every cell once, in order.
A non-blank cell goes to the next free slot of the kept prefix. Blank cells are skipped by not writing them.
The kept prefix. C reports its length through `returnSize`.

complexity.md: **Time O(n):** one read per cell, at most one write. **Space O(1)** besides the output.

steps.text: Read 4: not blank, write it at 0.
Read 7: not blank, write it at 1.
Read 3: not blank, write it at 2.
Read 8: not blank, write it at 3.
The first 4 cells are the answer: [4, 7, 3, 8].

walk.title: A read pointer visits every cell; a write pointer marks where the next kept cell goes.

takeaways.md:
- **Filter in place:** a reader visits everything, a writer collects what stays.
- The writer never passes the reader, so overwriting is safe.
- **Pitfall:** deleting with shifts (O(n²)).
